legend: The only difference between the easy version and the hard version is the constraint on n%%ZSMJ0%%.

Gunga just learned what a double-ended queue is in his data structure class. a double-ended queue (deque) is an abstract data type that generalizes a queue, for which elements can be added to or removed from either the front (head) or back (tail).

Now, he is playing with his own double-ended queue. He has an empty double-ended queue B%%ZSMJ1%% and an array of integers A%%ZSMJ2%%. In the i%%ZSMJ3%%-th move, he will add Ai%%ZSMJ4%% to one end of B%%ZSMJ5%%. This time, he wants to find the total sum of the sum of values BL%%ZSMJ6%% to BR%%ZSMJ7%% over all the 2n%%ZSMJ8%% possible B%%ZSMJ9%% formed. Since the answer can be large, output the answer \pmod{10^9+7}%%ZSMJ10%%. Two queues are considered different if Gunga's operation on some A_i%%ZSMJ11%% is different.
input: The first line contains an integer n,L,R%%ZSMJ12%% (1 \leq n \leq 5 \times 10^5,1\le L\le R\le n)%%ZSMJ13%% – the number of integers and Gunga's favorite interval.
The second line contains n%%ZSMJ14%% space-separated integers A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n%%ZSMJ15%% (-10^9 \leq A_i \leq 10^9)%%ZSMJ16%%.
note: In the first example, no matter which end of the queue Gunga adds the number to, the resulting queue will be [1,1,1,1,1]%%ZSMJ18%%. The total sum is 32\times(1+1+1+1+1)=160%%ZSMJ19%%.
The total sum of the sum of B_1%%ZSMJ23%% to B_2%%ZSMJ24%% is 2\times (1+2+2+1+3+2+3+1)=30%%ZSMJ25%%.
